transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Markus Voss (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (OrionApps ML Eng), Carlos Mendes (Eng Manager), Aisha Khan (Platform), Tom Reynolds (CTO)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscaling for OrionApps' conversational search workload. Discussed reserved GPUs for baseline throughput, burst strategy for peak traffic, fallback policies (smaller model or regional fallback), and success criteria (p50/p95 latency, throughput and cost targets). Action items: send sizing worksheet, run benchmarks, schedule PoC kickoff.

[00:00:10] Lena Park: Hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we have Markus from infra and me, and from OrionApps Priya, Carlos, Aisha and Tom right?
[00:00:22] Priya Patel: Yep that's right, thanks Lena.
[00:00:25] Carlos Mendes: Morning, hi all.
[00:00:28] Markus Voss: Hi. I'll be the technical lead on our end for the PoC.
[00:00:34] Tom Reynolds: Thanks for taking the time. We're mainly trying to validate cost and latency for a 6-week PoC.

[00:01:00] Lena Park: Great, goal for today is to nail down success criteria, get a first-pass on capacity sizing and autoscale approach, and confirm benchmarks and timeline. We'll capture next steps.

[00:02:15] Priya: Quick context - our workload is a conversational search/chat feature attached to our docs index. Typical session length is about 7-10 prompts per session, average prompt ~150 tokens, responses average 400-800 tokens depending on drilldown. Baseline concurrent active sessions is ~250 during business hours, spikes up to 1,200 during product launches.
[00:02:45] Carlos: Important: 80% of traffic is read-only inference (no private PII), but some queries hit internal docs with restricted content; we need VPC and KMS support for those routes.

[00:03:30] Markus: Good. For sizing we usually look at two things: steady reserved capacity for baseline SLA and burst pool for peaks. For a POC we can reserve a small pool of GPUs and allow burst to hosted capacity or extra reserved nodes.

[00:04:12] Aisha: Do you have recommendations for the GPU type? We run models in the ~7B-13B range (mix of Llama-like & instruction-tuned open models).
[00:04:28] Markus: For that model family we recommend testing on A100 80GB equivalent for quantized weights; many customers get good perf on 80GB A100 for 7-13B. We'll test both 2xA100 and 4xA100 configs for the PoC to see scaling.

[00:05:00] Lena: Also worth noting Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching, KV cache/prefix caching to improve throughput for repeated context — though transcript ASR sometimes writes it K V cash.

[00:05:22] Priya: Our main success criteria are: p50 latency under 400ms for short responses (<=200 tokens), p95 under 1.5s, and cost per 1k responses under $X (we gave a rough target in the RFP). We also care about session-level availability 99.9%.
[00:05:48] Markus: That aligns with what we've seen. Important to define what counts as a 'response' — we'll standardize on 400-token equivalent for cost calc. Also need representative prompt set for benchmarks.

[00:06:30] Tom: Timeline constraints — we'd like a PoC kickoff by week of 2025-05-19 and a 4-6 week execution window. Is that feasible?
[00:06:40] Lena: Yes that works if we get the worksheet and security checklist back this week. We'll also need your traffic distribution and sample prompts by 2025-05-09.

[00:07:10] Carlos: On autoscaling policy, what's the fastest you can spin up extra capacity in Redwood Dedicated? We've seen slow scale-ups elsewhere causing errors during big spikes.
[00:07:25] Markus: Two layers: reserved capacity (pre-provisioned GPUs) is instant for those replicas. For burst beyond reserved, we have two options — burst to pooled hosted capacity (fast, typically <60s to route but depends on model warmup) or pre-warm standby instances in a warm pool which we can schedule to reduce cold-starts (~30s). We can also fall back to a smaller, cheaper model variant if higher latency is acceptable.

[00:08:05] Priya: That warm pool approach sounds promising. For launches, our traffic ramp is often a few minutes, so 30-60s is acceptable, but we need graceful degradation during the spin-up.

[00:08:20] Markus: Exactly — fallback policies we propose: 1) automatic routing to a smaller model (e.g., 7B instead of 13B) with reduced context windows; 2) regional failover to another cluster; 3) rate limiting with informative 429 that triggers client-side retry/backoff. We can codify these in the PoC routing policy.

[00:09:00] Lena: On capacity math — if we assume 250 steady concurrency with average 400-token responses and a batch efficiency of ~1.8x due to repeated context, preliminary estimate is 2xA100 reserved should cover baseline with comfortable headroom, and 4xA100 for peak headroom to cover 1,200 spikes assuming burst pooling. But we need real benchmarks to confirm.

[00:09:45] Priya: Can you capture the assumptions you used? We need to show cost to finance.

[00:09:50] Lena: We'll put the assumptions in the sizing worksheet: avg tokens per response, batching factor, KV cache hit rate, concurrency, desired p95 target.

[00:10:20] Carlos: Benchmark plan — we want p50/p95 latency, tokens per second, and cost per 1k responses at both steady and spike loads. Also measure cold start times for model warmup.

[00:10:35] Markus: Proposed bench matrix: baseline test with 250 concurrency for 30 minutes, ramp test from 250 to 1,200 over 5 minutes, and a spike test hitting 1,200 for 10 minutes. For each test run A/B across 2xA100 reserved, 4xA100 reserved, and hosted-burst configuration. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latencies and throughput.

[00:11:15] Priya: We're most sensitive to p95 and cost during sustained spikes — for launches we care about maintaining a reasonable p95 rather than absolute p99.

[00:11:30] Aisha: Security question — for routes serving restricted docs we need private VPC peering and KMS integration so keys never leave our control.

[00:11:42] Lena: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering; for the PoC we can include private routes for sensitive traffic. We'll attach SOC 2 docs and the security FAQ.

[00:12:05] Tom: Any constraints around audit logs and retention? We need 1 year of detailed logs for compliance.

[00:12:12] Markus: Audit log retention is configurable; we can include that in the PoC as an optional add-on. We'll share the logging retention options in the security packet.

[00:12:40] Priya: A couple of practicals — how do you instrument the cache/kv hit rate and batching stats? We want visibility in the console to correlate latency drops with cache hits.

[00:12:55] Markus: Console shows per-model and per-route metrics: tokens/sec, batch size distribution, cache hit rate, per-token cost, and tail latencies. We can also stream traces to your tracing system.

[00:13:20] Lena: Ok let's talk about fallback tradeoffs. If we route to a smaller model during spikes, quality will drop. We need to define acceptable thresholds — e.g., if predicted latency >1.5s for p95 then fallback. That threshold should be configurable in the rollout policy for the PoC.

[00:13:50] Priya: We'll test quality degradation using a set of 200 test queries and human evals during the benchmark. If quality falls below X% we'll fail the fallback approach.

[00:14:10] Carlos: Cost controls — can you set budget caps to prevent runaway costs during the PoC?

[00:14:18] Lena: Yes, we can configure daily spend caps and alerting. For the PoC we'll recommend soft caps with alerts, and hard caps only if you want strict limits.

[00:14:40] Markus: A note on model warmup: if you have long context windows we recommend prefix caching to reduce warmup overhead for repeated system prompts. That can cut warmup tokens significantly.

[00:15:00] Tom: For the burst pool, is capacity shared across customers? Is there any noisy neighbor risk?

[00:15:08] Markus: The hosted burst pool is multi-tenant but isolated at the runtime level; performance isolation is strong but not absolute. For strict isolation we recommend reserved capacity or Dedicated clusters. For the PoC we can run a dedicated small pool to minimize noisy neighbor risk.

[00:15:40] Priya: Regarding metrics, we need to see per-route cost attribution so we can map features to spend.

[00:15:48] Lena: Console provides token-level cost attribution down to route and model. We'll include screenshots in the follow-up.

[00:16:05] Carlos: Any gotchas we should be aware of?

[00:16:12] Markus: One is sequence length mismatch: if a few queries require long context it skews batching; we'd recommend a max context cap for latency-sensitive routes and optionally background retrieval for long-doc queries. Also watch KV cache TTLs — too short and you lose hits, too long and you store stale context.

[00:16:45] Priya: For benchmark tooling, can you run the workload that replays our 24-hour traffic distribution?

[00:16:52] Markus: Yes, we'll replay traffic shape. Please provide sample logs and distribution. The more representative, the better the sizing.

[00:17:20] Lena: Let's confirm the PoC variants we will test: (A) 2xA100 reserved baseline with warm pool, (B) 4xA100 reserved for peak, (C) reserved 2xA100 + hosted burst routing, (D) smaller-model fallback policy. Does that capture it?

[00:17:38] Priya: Yes.

[00:17:40] Carlos: Also run a config with slightly higher batching aggressiveness to see cost tradeoffs — though that may increase latency variance.

[00:17:55] Markus: We'll include a batching profile sweep in the bench matrix.

[00:18:10] Tom: Can you outline success criteria one more time so we can align internally?

[00:18:18] Lena: Sure. Agreed success criteria for the PoC: 1) p50 < 400ms for short responses, p95 < 1.5s for standard responses; 2) cost per 1k responses below target provided in RFP (we'll convert to $/token in follow-up); 3) autoscale behavior: cold-starts <60s with warm pool <30s, and graceful fallback that keeps p95 under 3s during spikes; 4) security: private VPC/KMS for restricted routes; 5) observability: route-level metrics and cost attribution available in console.

[00:19:05] Priya: That looks good. We'll add quality acceptance thresholds after we run the human evals.

[00:19:25] Lena: Next steps recap: I'll send the sizing worksheet + security packet by 2025-05-09. Markus will run the benchmark matrix and share results by 2025-05-13. We'll target PoC kickoff week of 2025-05-19. Customer to provide prompt set and traffic shape by 2025-05-09.

[00:20:00] Carlos: One more question — do you support canary rollouts during PoC? We want to test canary vs full route switch.

[00:20:08] Markus: Yes, rollout policies support canary %, A/B, and automatic rollback based on error or latency thresholds. We'll demo that in the PoC.

[00:20:30] Priya: Anything else on networking? We may need IP allowlist and private egress.

[00:20:37] Lena: We'll include IP allowlist and VPC peering instructions in the security doc.

[00:21:00] Tom: Okay thanks — looks like we're aligned.

[00:21:05] Lena: Great. I'll follow up with the worksheet and calendar invite for kickoff. Any final questions?

[00:21:12] Aisha Khan: Not from me.

[00:21:15] Priya: All good.

[00:21:18] Carlos: Thanks.

[00:21:20] Markus: Thanks everyone.

[00:21:40] Speaker 1: (background) we'll capture those logs.

[00:22:00] END OF RECORDING
